content: Public and Private Folklore: The Function of Folk-Culture in The Return of the Native and Jude the Obscure Jude Wright Victorians: A Journal of Culture and Literature, Number 137, Summer 2020, pp. 30-43 (Article) Published by The Ohio State University Press DOI: For additional information about this article [ Access provided at 25 Oct 2020 06:19 GMT from Fondren Library, Rice University ] https://doi.org/10.1353/vct.2020.0000 https://muse.jhu.edu/article/760993

Victorians: A Journal of Culture and Literature No. 137 (Summer 2020) Copyright © 2020 by The Ohio State University Public and Private Folklore: The Function of Folk-Culture in The Return of the Native and Jude the Obscure JUDE WRIGHT ABSTRACT: Thomas Hardy’s use of folklore in his novels is best understood as a drama­ tization of characters’ tendencies towards meaning-making, seen also in the poems “The Convergence of the Twain” and “Ah, Are You Digging on my Grave.” Hardy’s process of meaning-making attempts to impose some order on chance happenings (or “haps”). Drawing on Bill Ellis’s discussions of the purpose and utility of folklore in daily life, this essay examines the ways that folkloric narrative framing functions in the public or com­ munal folklore of The Return of the Native and in the private or family folklore present in Jude the Obscure. In each, Hardy utilizes folklore to dramatize human meaning-making in the face of an indifferent universe. KEYWORDS: folklore, folk-culture hermeneutics, Jude the Obscure, Return of the Native, Thomas Hardy, Victorian literature, Hardy’s poetry REVIEWERS AND CRITICS HAVE consistently commented on the ways that Thomas Hardy’s poems and novels capture the texture of folk-life in his imaginary “dream-country” of Wessex (Hardy, Preface 3). Ruth A. Firor carefully catalogued the astonishing range of Hardy’s references in Folkways in Thomas Hardy (1931); subsequent critics examined the role these references play in his texts. While folk-culture as presented in his writing adds texture, as Betty Rich Lombardi notes, Hardy did not see himself as an ethnographer

Folk-Culture in The Return of the Native and Jude the Obscure 31 preserving the folk-life of his native Dorset. This essay argues that Hardy uses folklore as a hermeneutic through which humans create narrative order out of chaos; he dramatizes the process of meaning-making as characters confront seemingly random or chance hap­ penings—“haps,” as he termed them. Such an emphasis links Hardy’s use of folklore to his larger tendencies towards interpretive framing. Folklore is one strategy he utilizes to present this kind of dramatization, and as such is part of his overall interest in the construction of meaning. Backward Gazes and Interpretive Frameworks Hardy’s earliest poem, “Domicilium,” begins with a description of the ordered, picturesque natural world surrounding a rural cottage. Initially, the setting is situated in the present, then moves back in time to the land as described by the narrator’s grandmother, his “fa­ ther’s mother” (l. 20), providing a much different vision of the landscape. From the depths of her memory, the grandmother summons up an uncultivated setting that pre-figures the present order: Yonder garden-plots And orchards were uncultivated slopes O’ergrown with bramble bushes, furze and thorn: That road a narrow path shut in by ferns, Which, almost trees, obscured the passer-by. (ll. 26–30) The grandmother’s vision represents both the world that was and its implications for the world that is. As memory must do, it conceives of the past in relation to the present, layer­ ing the present day orchards, garden-plots, and road onto the past, when they did not yet exist. The wild woodland that once surrounded the house is viewed through a hermeneutic in relation to the present setting.1 This backward gaze, what J. Hillis Miller has called “a retrospective consciousness,” is a primary element in Hardy’s poetry (344). Written half a century after “Domicilium,” “The Convergence of the Twain: Lines Written upon the Sinking of the Titanic” also relies on this kind of backward gaze for its essential meaning. It famously begins with the rusting hulk of the colossal ship on the ocean floor, and then describes the simultaneous construction of the ship, the formation of the iceberg, and the fateful collision of the two. Tim Armstrong notes that the poem’s structure appears “to suggest that the causes of events can only be known in a post hoc fashion” (32). Understanding this cause and effect requires an inter­ 1. The title “Domicilium” further points to its construction as a controlled kind of meaning-making, one superimposed on a more organic memory in order to give it shape and structure. Reading the poem biographically, “There is one oddity, in his giving [the poem] its Latin title, ‘Domicilium’ (meaning ‘Home’). Latin would have been meaningless to Granny Hardy. It is here an offering from one side of his divided self to the other” (Tomalin 56). This may be seen as Hardy placing the memory within the larger context of his Latin-reading poetic life.

32 Jude Wright pretive framing of the events that ascribes meaning based upon outcome, meanings that are only available in interpretive retrospect through the backward gaze. This layering of time is a well-known characteristic of Hardy’s work, particularly his poetry,2 with the backward gaze functioning as a dramatization of meaning-making. The post hoc vision of the cause in “The Convergence of the Twain”—acts generated by an “Immanent Will” (l. 18) and the “Spinner of the Years” (l. 31)—metatextually points to how humans construe events, in order to give them shape and meaning. It is only through a knowledge of the Titanic’s fate that the kind of narrative (including divine, if ambiguous, figures) the poem presents can be constructed. Examining either the ship or the iceberg at any other point in their trajectories provides no indication of their connection. The meaning of both only becomes clear in that “august event” (l. 30) when “consummation comes, and jars two hemispheres” (l. 33). The poem leads us to examine the process by which humans make meaning out of seemingly random events.3 This kind of interpretive meaning-making is a quality of public—in the case of the Titanic—and personal—as in the example from “Domicilium”—history in Hardy; it also demonstrates how humans seek to establish meaning in a world the author casts as essen­ tially meaningless. In “Ah, Are You Digging on My Grave,” a dead woman addresses one who is digging on her grave, seeking both to identify the digger and to find meaning in this puzzling event. She makes her way through various associates—her lover, her family, her enemy—trying to determine who it is that disturbs her rest. She is relieved to learn it is her dog, which provides the event with meaning: “Ah yes! You dig upon my grave . . . Why flashed it not on me That one true heart was left behind! What feeling do we ever find To equal among human kind A dog’s fidelity!” (ll. 25–30) The dead woman interprets the dog’s digging as filled with meaning, constructing the events through a hermeneutic informed by her desire to be loved and remembered. With a great deal of irony, however, Hardy’s dog undercuts his posthumous speaker’s assumptions about fidelity: “Mistress, I dug upon your grave To bury a bone, in case 2. J. Hillis Miller notes the abundant criticism focused on Hardy’s relationship to time. Martin Middeke notes: “In a circular fashion, the consciousness of Hardy’s characters is replete with memories of their being tortured by their past, which mercilessly falls back on them. Especially Hardy’s later fiction is distinguished by an excruciating sensibility for the destructive weight of the past and by the impression of an indifferent flow of time, which appears hostile to all individual endeavors to read meaning into life” (115). 3. The Titanic was immersed in this meaning-making from the moment of its launch, which increased in gravity upon its sinking. See Paul Heyer’s Titanic Legacy: Disaster as Media Event and Myth (West Port, CT: Praeger, 1995).

Folk-Culture in The Return of the Native and Jude the Obscure 33 I should be hungry near this spot When passing on my daily trot. I am sorry, but I quite forgot It was your resting-place.” (ll. 31–36) This is a darkly humorous example of Hardy’s meaning-making, wherein humans superim­ pose order and narrative significance on events that are, in effect, random and meaningless.4 Deborah L. Collins argues that, in his novels, Hardy purposefully set accidentalism against the background of folk ritual in order to demonstrate that designless, specifically Darwinian happenings have evolved a human context in which the odds for survival can be calculated and adaptive strategies implemented. If coincidences appear demonically instigated, it is because society, thrown off centre, assigns them a negative value based on their power to disrupt ordinary routine. Likewise, if readers insist on attributing naturalist values to Hardy’s use of natural accidents, it is because they, too, are uncomfortable with what appears to be “Crass Casualty.” (100) This setting of accident in the context of human-created patterns illustrates how Hardy’s characters and readers seek order in disorder and construct meaning out of random events. In both his novels and poetry, meaning is generated by superimposing an interpretive framework on events that may have no connection or wherein the connection is unclear or unavailable. Just as the woman in “Ah, Are You Digging on My Grave” interprets the dog’s motive and the meaning of his actions incorrectly to serve her desires, Hardy’s use of folklore and supernatural elements help make sense of chaos, turning a mere “hap” into the deliberate actions of the “Spinner of the Years.” This is illustrated by several similar in­ terpretive discourses: the magical worldviews represented in The Return of the Native, and Jude Fawley’s “cursed” family history in Jude the Obscure. In each novel, multi-layered con­ fluences of events, products of human desire, human cruelty, and the operations of chance are given order by an interpretive principle superimposed upon the events themselves. The Function of Folklore Hardy’s investment in and use of folklore has been extensively discussed, beginning with Firor’s work and continuing through such critics as Andrew Radford, Tom Nash, and Gayla R. Steel. Folklore is woven into the fabric of Hardy’s fiction through both individual di­ alogue—especially community conversations—and third-person narrative. Yet as has also been noted, principally by Lombardi, Hardy’s concern is not precisely that of an ethnogra­ pher, no matter how fascinating or vivid his representations of these folkways are. Lombardi notes that the novelist’s collection methods were enthusiastic, but not comprehensive: 4. This randomness is aptly expressed in Hardy’s “Hap,” where all events, good or bad, are attributed to “Crass Casualty” (11).

34 Jude Wright The lore which Hardy uses in his Wessex novels was collected in a rather haphaz­ ard way. He recorded snatches of songs in his notebooks, beliefs and remedies on the back of old envelopes, paying no attention whatsoever to his informant . . . This is no unusual revelation about Thomas Hardy, for he was so at home in the Wessex region that his imagination was free to work upon material thoroughly familiar to him for a lifetime. (20) Lombardi suggests that Hardy utilizes folk-life to add shape and texture to his imaginative Wessex, which is a far different project than the chronicling of those folkways.5 In using these elements, Hardy points to how they shape characters’ interactions with and under­ standing of the world, demonstrating a use of folk-materials that goes beyond presenting local color or narrative structure. In seeking a productive relationship between folk-studies and literary studies, Tom Nash focuses on the function of folklore in Hardy’s Tess of the D’Urbervilles. Rather than viewing Tess as a vehicle for folk-culture, Nash emphasizes its narrative significance: “It is a mistake to see Tess of the D’Urbervilles either as a prose version of the ballad or as a sim­ ple tragedy. In fact Hardy is telling a story as old as Stonehenge itself: the myth of birth, death, and regeneration. Although the folklore clearly presages Tess’s death, Hardy makes that death a ritual” (44). Nash also argues that those who focus on the novel’s interest in tragedy miss the true significance of its folklore: “Tess is not a Greek Tragedy; indeed, not a tragedy at all. In stressing Tess’s execution and Angel’s loss, the critics ignore the scene taking place at the summit of the great West Hill overlooking the site of execution” (45). That is the scene involving Angel and Tess’s sister Liza-Lu, which represents the culmination of the folkloric death and rebirth motif, a reading which makes ironic sense of the tragedy or, as Nash insists, turns the narrative from tragedy to myth. Hardy’s intricate use of folk­ lore enables such a reading, exemplifying the idea of meaning-making that is the subject of this paper. Nash’s reading of Tess is part of his larger concern with the disjunction between literary studies and folklore, in which literary scholars fail to properly recognize folklore’s “function” in literature (40). But function does not fully account for the role of folklore in Hardy’s novels, where it creates a hermeneutic that lends order to chaotic events. Acts of chance—like Tring­ ham’s remark to Durbeyfield about the origin of his surname, or the fatal accident with the horse—imply an order underpinning the chaos.6 The same dynamic occurs in The Return of the Native, where folklore ranges from the history of the heath to Susan Nunsuch’s wax effigy. The novel’s events exhibit a confluence of chance encounters, human emotions, and ill-luck, yet such folkloric devices dramatize how humans seek meaning in what is, from Hardy’s nihilistic perspective, ultimately meaningless. It is important to note, however, that this is—according to folklore theorists—the very function it serves in life, as well as in fiction. Bill Ellis, critic and chronicler of contemporary 5. How Hardy (and other writers) incorporates folklore and anthropology helped shaped the discourses of those disciplines invites further investigation. 6. Tragedy as a genre with its own rules and conventions also functions as a way to impose order on chaos.

Folk-Culture in The Return of the Native and Jude the Obscure 35 folklore, points to the need that folklore serves in its immediate context—for example, the social function of legends: One role of the legend is to redefine reality in a way that restores the narrators’ control over situations. This is what I call “the Rumpelstiltskin Principle.” That is, an ambiguous situation produces stress until witnesses find a “name” or a state­ ment of it in acceptable cultural language. Once this is done, the experience can be translated into a narrative and shared with others, and the act of narrating gives the observers power over the event. When the princess guessed Rumpel­ stiltskin’s name, she reduced his uncanny nature to words and saved her child by giving her magical power over the threat. (Aliens xiv) Ellis outlines a process similar to the backwards gaze in “The Convergence of the Twain.” The traumatic event of the Titanic’s sinking is made intelligible through imposing the cul­ tural language of a pre-destined cause. The event is, in a sense, “named,” as Ellis would say: “A major function of legends, then, is to serve, individually and collectively, as convenient language for the experiences that lie, actually or potentially, at the very boundaries of ex­ istence” (62). Legends and other associated folklore serve the function of making an inco­ herent world coherent for individuals and communities. This purpose is not unique to the current moment, but rather is a larger part of how folklore functions and why it thrives. Hardy is keenly aware of the role that these stories, allusions, and associations play in shap­ ing humans’ understanding of the world around them. As Gayla R. Steel puts it: “Hardy’s understanding that the tyrants and goblins emanate from the human psyche helps make him one of the most forward looking writers of the late Victorian era” (2).7 These figures have their origins in the psyche, but they function to provide a means to interpret an often incoherent reality. Witchcraft on the Heath: The Return of the Native The opening scenes of The Return of the Native exemplify this meaning-making dynamic, ranging from building the bonfire on Egdon Heath to other fires burning across the coun­ tryside. Regarding Egdon Heath, “Not a plough had ever disturbed a grain of that stubborn soil. In the heath’s barrenness to the farmer lay its fertility to the historian. There had been no obliteration, because there had been no tending” (20). The heath, and the men and women who live and work there, is cast as unchanging; in this way, the meaning of people’s lives may be interpreted by looking backwards through history, evident in both landscape and customs. This is juxtaposed, at least implicitly, with the wider world represented by 7. Ellis’s work provides telling examples about the way folklore in contemporary culture shapes how humans think about the world around them. He writes for instance of “Rumor-Panic” surrounding legends of satanic cults as “therapeutic magic” (“Devil Worshippers” 27). Hardy’s fictions represent the process by which this interpretation happens, dramatizing how meaning is established based on folk belief and religious belief, and where the two intersect.

36 Jude Wright places like Budmouth (the bustling sea-side resort town Eustacia Vye hails from) and sug­ gests that this seemingly unchanging rural space provides some anchor in the midst of a changing modern world. Hardy connects the bonfire to pagan festivities of the historical past: It was as if these men and boys had suddenly dived into past ages, and fetched therefrom an hour and deed which had before been familiar with this spot. The ashes of the original British pyre which blazed from that summit lay fresh and undisturbed in the barrow beneath their tread. The flames from funeral piles long ago kindled there had shone down upon the lowlands as these were shining now. Festival fires to Thor and Woden had followed on the same ground and duly had their day. Indeed, it is pretty well known that such blazes as this the heathmen were now enjoying are rather the lineal descendants from jumbled Druidical rites and Saxon ceremonies than the invention of popular feeling about Gunpowder Plot. (20–21) The backward-gaze of this paragraph does significant interpretive work. It connects the modern tradition of Guy Fawkes Night back far earlier than its seventeenth-century incep­ tion, placing it within a pagan historical lineage. A larger order is imposed on the event than is warranted by the local custom, or indeed by the understandings of the characters celebrating bonfire night. Hardy goes further, however, than superimposing a kind of pre-Christian meaning upon the national holiday. He roots it in the nature of humanity itself, as a kind of universal touchstone drawn from multiple discourses, mythic and seasonal: Moreover to light a fire is the instinctive and resistant act of man when, at the winter ingress, the curfew is sounded throughout Nature. It indicates a sponta­ neous, Promethean rebelliousness against that fiat that this recurrent season shall bring foul times, cold darkness, misery and death. Black chaos comes, and the fettered gods of the earth say, Let there be light. (21) In terms of significance to a hermeneutic reading, Hardy here clearly takes not only a con­ temporary custom, but also a narrative event, thus creating a framework lending that event greater significance. This is a significance that transcends time and place—a universal “Let there be light” blending the Jewish and Christian traditions of Genesis with the “Promet­ hean” imagery of Greco-Roman mythology, placed in a seasonal framework stretching back to earliest, primitive humanity. An interesting irony here is that Hardy’s rustics do not seem aware of the kind of mythic signification he invokes. Andrew Radford notes this disconnect, while carefully distinguishing Hardy’s third-person narrator from Hardy himself: The bonfire-lighting productively underscores the gulf between “history” and “heritage” in Hardy’s narrative. The local historian assesses with painstaking pre­

Folk-Culture in The Return of the Native and Jude the Obscure 37 cision those bygone times which have become utterly remote from and alien to contemporary experience. The purveyor of heritage by contrast posits that for­ saken or forgotten fragments bespeak an urgent presence, an informing and be­ neficent spirit whose role is to enrich the modern moment and shape the future. Hardy’s antiquarian narrator may laud and campaign for a heritage epitomized by the tangible grandeur of Rainbarrow. But it is doubtful whether the Egdon “men and boys” possess, or would wish to acquire, such knowledge of art objects, institutions, tribal rituals and sacred traditions. (25–26) This is best read not as a class judgment—for Hardy presents his rural men and women in sympathetic and complicated ways—but as a product of his hermeneutics. That is, such a judgment is external to the men and women involved in the celebration; it is the third-person narrator’s attempt to make sense of the actions of this and other communities across a broad scope of human history. Recent work by Ronald Hutton and other historians notes how little connection there is between the Guy Fawkes celebrations and earlier pagan worship.8 As such, it can be seen precisely how much imaginative framing links the bonfire ritual with Celtic and Norse rit­ ual. Hardy appears to be aware that, by invoking these folkloric connections, he superim­ poses larger meaning on a contemporary, historically-specific event—an ironic disjunction between participants and history. Bonfire Night returns at the novel’s end as the evening when Eustacia and Wildeve are to leave Egdon together, leading to the novel’s tragic conclusion. This repetition helps to structure the narrative, while providing another dramatization of meaning-making through folk-custom. Hardy’s characters utilize this to envision a kind of supernatural shape to such symmetry, a destiny that unfolds from fire-festival to fire-festival. However, this kind of understanding is subordinated to a larger concern: the very human associations the char­ acters make with the bonfire festivities. It should not be surprising that it is this night, the one marking Eustacia’s doomed affair with Wildeve, on which she becomes agitated, cannot control her passion, and decides to leave. This kind of meaning goes further in Hardy’s usage of Susan Nunsuch’s wax effigy of Eustacia. The Return of the Native is not alone in its invocation of a wax effigy as means of constructing meaning out of randomness. In The Mayor of Casterbridge, Michael Henchard considers whether his misfortunes might find their origin in just such as device: “‘I won­ der,’ he asked himself with eerie misgiving; ‘I wonder if it can be that somebody has been roasting a waxen image of me, or stirring an unholy brew to confound me! I don’t believe in such power; and yet—what if they should ha’ been doing it!’” (Mayor 190). Ultimately, however, the source of Henchard’s travails is revealed to be quite mundane. The wax doll sequence in The Return of the Native is presented with a great deal of convincing detail, as “Susan Nunsuch literally charms her enemy Eustacia to death” (Firor 86). However, Hardy’s presentation of this superstition is not so straightforward, as close attention to his language suggests. Nunsuch herself provides a perfect example of the dy­ 8. See Ronald Hutton, The Stations of the Sun: A History of the Ritual Year in Britain (Oxford: Oxford UP, 1996 [393–407]).

38 Jude Wright namic of interpretive framing under discussion here, given that she reacts to what is in reality Eustacia’s simple wandering: Eustacia could not rest indoors, having nothing more to do, and she wandered to and fro on the hill, not far from the house she was soon to leave. In these desul­ tory ramblings she passed the cottage of Susan Nunsuch, a little lower down than her grandfather’s. The door was ajar, and a riband of bright firelight fell over the ground without. As Eustacia crossed the firebeams she appeared for an instant as distinct as a figure in a phantasmagoria—a creature of light surrounded by an area of darkness; the moment passed, and she was absorbed in night again. A woman who was sitting inside the cottage had seen and recognized her in that momentary irradiation. This was Susan herself, occupied in preparing a pos­ set for her little boy, who, often ailing, was now seriously unwell. Susan dropped the spoon, shook her fist at the vanished figure, and then proceeded with her work in a musing, absent way. (337) The reader understands that this chance encounter is innocent, yet Nunsuch views it is proof of a supernatural threat and crafts the wax doll in response: “Susan’s sight of her passing figure earlier in the evening, not five minutes after the sick boy’s exclamation, ‘Mother, I do feel so bad!’ persuaded the matron that an evil influence was certainly exercised by Eusta­ cia’s propinquity” (342). Superstition and folk-belief are here utilized to explain the unex­ plainable; but, ironically, Nunsuch’s interpretation rests on the chance sighting of Eustacia, a chance similar to many others found in Hardy’s fiction. Hardy’s initial statement about the image is interesting in its studied ambivalence: To counteract the malign spell which she imagined poor Eustacia to be working, the boy’s mother busied herself with a ghastly invention of superstition, calculat­ ed to bring powerlessness, atrophy, and annihilation on any human being against whom it was directed. It was a practice well known on Egdon at that date, and one that is not quite extinct at the present day. (342) Nunsuch’s interpretation of Eustacia as malevolent witch is a fantasy; thus the wax image is “a ghastly invention of superstition,” while at the same time giving the superstition an amount of power in naming what it is “calculated” to achieve. Hardy details the creation of the wax figure, as if encouraging readers’ focus on it as the cause of Eustacia’s downfall. The fact that her death occurs in the next chapter also lends the cause and effect relationship some credence. However, Yeobright then undercuts the supernatural explanation: “Why should it be she? Because last week she would have put an end to her life if she had been able. She ought to have been watched!” (355). Eustacia’s death was foreshadowed by her suicidal depression, a depression that certainly pre-dates Nunsuch’s witchcraft and is of course driven by her own restricted circumstances. Nunsuch’s magic functions as a way of understanding Eustacia’s death that elides the social problems and crass casualty that inter­ twine to create her tragic end. It provides drama of course, and carries with it an intensity

Folk-Culture in The Return of the Native and Jude the Obscure 39 that is impressive; but it functions as a hermeneutic applied after the fact, lending meaning to complicated and haphazard events.9 The Private Folklore of the Fawley Family Curse The Return of the Native is framed by public folk-belief on a literal and figurative level, the novel beginning and ending with bonfire night celebrations on Egdon Heath. Jude the Obscure shifts somewhat in its representation of folklore, moving from a public folklore as the interpretive framing that creates order out of chaos to a more personal one.10 While Hardy’s readers can be expected to understand the multifaceted institutional barriers to his protagonists’ happiness as a confluence of rigid social structures, personality quirks, and indeed chance, Jude himself envisions the root cause as a family curse that has haunted his bloodline for generations. This personal or private folklore concerns the legend of the family’s general unfitness for marriage, here conveyed to eleven-year-old Jude by his aunt: My niece and her husband, after they were married, didn’ get a house of their own for some year or more; and then they only had one till—Well, I won’t go into that. Jude, my child, don’t you ever marry. ’Tisn’t for the Fawleys to take that step any more. She, their only one, was like a child o’ my own, Belinda, till the split come! Ah, that a little maid should know such changes! (8) Conchita Díez-Medrano notes how this family curse draws from post-Darwinian concepts of biological inheritance, casting Jude and Sue’s family malady as a kind of biological family folklore. It is focused on heredity, but it also provides a venue for meaning-making that allows the family, including Jude and Sue, to make sense of the crass-casualty of their situ­ ations (49–52). A number of critics have followed Hardy’s suggestion, reading this piece of family lore as evidence of Jude’s biological degeneracy, and reading the novel as an expres­ sion of late-Victorian anxieties about degeneration, biological and cultural.11 While cousin marriage was common in the Victorian era—Queen Victoria herself was married to Prince 9. Hardy both links and disassociates Eustacia with witchcraft. She is seemingly one with the heath: “There the form stood, motionless as the hill beneath. Above the plain rose the hill, above the hill rose the barrow, and above the barrow rose the figure. Above the figure was nothing that could be mapped elsewhere than on a celestial globe,” and thus connected to the harsh primitive land like the witch of lore (17). But she also represents a strange juxtaposition between nature and culture: “Egdon was her Hades, and since coming there she had imbibed much of what was dark in its tone, though inwardly and eternally unreconciled thereto . . . Why did a woman of this sort live on Egdon Heath? Budmouth was her native place, a fashionable seaside resort at that date” (67–68). 10. There are numerous examples of public folklore in Jude as well, but an examination of these is outside of the scope of this article. 11. See William Greenslade, Degeneration, Culture and the Novel 1880–1940 (Cambridge: Cambridge UP, 1994), who argues for a complicated relationship between degeneration as presented on the surface level of the novel and larger, more subversive concerns. Still he reads the hereditary unfitness as somewhere between a family myth and a real condition (151–81). See also Sondra Archimedes, Gendered Pathologies: The Female

40 Jude Wright Albert, her first cousin—“there was a persistent undercurrent of concern about close con­ sanguineal marriage” (Kuper 167). As post-Darwinian scientific discourses evolved, such hereditary concerns grew more acute: indeed, fears that cousin-marriages produced infirm or disabled children mingled with and fed into fin de siècle obsessions with degeneration. However, this focus on degeneration in Jude is not actually coherent in itself, but rather functions as a meaning-making strategy by which Jude’s family and Jude himself make sense of the complicated randomness of the universe. Both Jude and Sue frame the failure of their marriages (Jude’s to Arabella and Sue’s to Philotson) through this familial legend, and it is not surprising that one of its most im­ portant articulations finds prime interpretive real-estate: Sue’s knowledge of the personal folklore is made apparent just before she announces, via letter, her impending nuptials with Philotson. Jude begins the dialogue by telling her of his aunt’s statements: “. . . . it was always impressed upon me that I ought not to marry—that I belonged to an odd and peculiar family—the wrong breed for marriage.” “Ah—who used to say that to you?” “My great-aunt. She said it always ended badly with us Fawleys.” “That’s strange. My father used to say the same to me!” They stood possessed by the same thought, ugly enough, even as an assump­ tion: that a union between them, had such been possible, would have meant a terrible intensification of unfitness—two bitters in one dish. “Oh, but there can’t be anything in it!” she said with nervous lightness. “Our family have been unlucky of late years in choosing mates—that’s all.” And then they pretended to persuade themselves that all that had happened was of no consequence, and that they could still be cousins and friends and warm correspondents, and have happy genial times when they met, even if they met less frequently than before. Their parting was in good friendship, and yet Jude’s last look into her eyes was tinged with inquiry, for he felt that he did not even now quite know her mind. (161) Thus, in Jude’s eyes, his bad marriage to Arabella was not due to the mundane heat of his youthful passion and her cold calculation but, rather, rooted in this family curse. Jude berates himself for not heeding the familial warning, but does not go further than that in criticizing his own poor judgment. Sue’s response, characterized by “nervous lightness,” reveals that this familial folklore lurks in her own psyche, anticipating a rationale for the dissolution of her forthcoming marriage to Philotson. But the hereditary family curse is never a satisfactory explanation, despite what Jude and Sue think, and Hardy consistently takes great pains to point out disparities between their fears and actual reality. Emily Steinlight sums this up excellently: Body and Biomedical Discourse in the Nineteenth-Century English Novel (New York: Routledge, 2005). Archi­ medes reads Sue’s neurosis as an expression of larger cultural concerns with degeneracy (125–55).

Folk-Culture in The Return of the Native and Jude the Obscure 41 Hardy’s language crackles with the dissonance of what it yokes together in voicing Jude’s and Sue’s unspoken fears that “a union between them . . . would have meant a terrible intensification of unfitness—two bitters in one dish.” Note the idiomatic slippage, in this sentence, from the discourse of heredity to that of the homely cliché. The propositions of biology have the ring of iron laws of necessity, but their explanatory power never quite suffices in the absence of metaphor. They are insistently recast in figurative language and often analogized: a double move that embeds their abstract authority in the concrete obviousness of the everyday while rendering them indistinguishable from rumor, superstition, and aphorism. (231) Hardy’s narrative does not ultimately support the curse as an explanation, even if it turns out to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, as far as Jude and Sue are concerned. Hardy further folklorizes the family curse by providing a possible origin for the belief. This is recounted by Mrs. Edlin, who is not entirely clear about its precise connection to the Fawleys: She ran away from him, with their child, to her friends; and while she was there the child died. He wanted the body, to bury it where his people lay, but she wouldn’t give it up. Her husband then came in the night with a cart, and broke into the house to steal the coffin away; but he was catched, and being obstinate, wouldn’t tell what he broke in for. They brought it in burglary, and that’s why he was hanged and gibbeted on Brown House Hill. His wife went mad after he was dead. But it medn’t be true that he belonged to ye more than to me. (272) This recalls Aunt Drusilla’s earlier passing remark about the place where Jude’s parents parted: “where the road to Fenworth branches off, and the handpost stands. A gibbet once stood there not unconnected with our history” (65). This episode is a well-constructed origin for the familial legend of a curse, with its elements of broken marriage, death of a child, execution, and madness. Hardy here provides a possible explanation for all of the negativity surrounding marriage that plagues the Faw­ ley and Bridehead families. It is also interestingly distanced from both the novel’s present, and the familial trouble Hardy describes earlier: the parting of Jude’s parents. The event occurred “in my grandfather’s time,” says Mrs. Edlin (272). This distancing undercuts the curse interpretation, as it is perhaps not so unusual to have these bad marriages occurring at various points throughout several generations. However, Sue and Jude do not see this episode as an origin that explains the family legend. Rather, they both interpret the story as further proof that there is in fact something supernatural at work. Sue states, “It makes me feel as if a tragic doom overhung our family, as it did the house of Atreus,” while Jude suggests “the house of Jeroboam” (273).12 This link to another cursed family line solidifies the idea of supernaturalism rather than the tragic collisions of desire, chance, and social judgment. In the end, Jude’s fatalistic resignation to 12. This is another interesting hermeneutic moment. Sue the Hellenist, with her statues of Venus and Apollo, draws from Greek Mythology, while Jude with his memorized scripture invokes the Old Testament.

42 Jude Wright death conveys a kind of dark providence that seems connected to the family curse: “I have seen her for the last time, and I’ve finished myself—put an end to a feverish life which ought never to have been begun!” (380). Despite asserting that his view is informed by “the grind of stern reality,” Jude pinpoints his very birth into this bloodline as the origin of his troubles, not the various incidents of chance and passion that led him to his early grave. Hardy’s representation of folk-culture is one of the most interesting aspects of his work. It is part of what makes his imaginary Wessex feel so developed and real. However, it is part of a larger strategy he utilized to dramatize and examine the ways humans construct meaning. Hardy’s presentation of folklore serves as one facet of this larger interest, an inter­ est so prominent that it might be called one of his major projects. Like the backward-gaze in “Domicilium” and “The Convergence of the Twain,” folklore for Hardy functions as a hermeneutic through which human beings construct meaning out of the chaos of existence. This is as true of the communal folklore of Egdon Heath’s residents as it is of the private family tradition of the Fawleys. Folklore in Hardy functions to name the unnamable, give shape to the shapeless, and give meaning to the “crass casualty” that shapes his universe.
